result: The authors developed a training protocol for head-fixed mice to navigate VR environments on a treadmill, requiring approximately 10-14 days of training with water rewards. The protocol resulted in about 40% of mice meeting criteria to advance to the experimental stage, with attrition occurring primarily when the tail-coat was added and water rewards were removed.
evaluation: Reviewers acknowledged the training protocol as part of the 'fundamental design' which is 'strong,' though they noted the 40% attrition rate as a limitation. One reviewer stated 'high rates of activity in the VR environment is crucial for detecting learning-related freezing' and acknowledged that 'it is possible that further adjustments to the procedure could improve attrition rates.' Another reviewer noted the 'extended training and attrition rate' as a weakness, indicating the paradigm 'requires weeks of training and only 40% of mice reach criteria.'

result: Three paradigms were developed varying the familiarity of control environments and shock parameters. Paradigm 1 used a familiar training environment as control and a novel environment for CFC; Paradigms 2 and 3 used two novel environments. Paradigms differed in tail-coat presence during recall and inter-shock intervals. Mice received 4-12 shocks at 0.5-1 mA with consistent immediate increases in running speed following shocks.
evaluation: Reviewers explicitly discussed the three paradigm variations, with one stating 'Paradigm versions 1 and 2 vary the familiarity of the control context while paradigm versions 2 and 3 vary the inter-shock interval.' The experimental design and shock parameters were accepted without critique, indicating reviewer support for these methodological claims.

result: In Paradigm 1, mice showed similar behavior in both VR environments before fear conditioning, but after CFC displayed significant increases in freezing and time to complete laps in the CFC VR compared to the Familiar VR on recall Day 1. Freezing was especially pronounced during the first lap, with behaviors including slowing down, freezing, moving backward, and hesitation to move forward.
evaluation: Reviewers explicitly endorsed Paradigm 1 results, stating 'Version 1 is the most promising, showing the greatest increase in conditioned freezing (~40%) and good discrimination between contexts (delta ~15-20%).' The editor's assessment noted 'solid evidence supports the claim that the reported methods provide a reliable paradigm' and that 'head-fixed mice exhibited freezing behavior in response to an aversive stimulus in VR, consistent with conditioned responses seen in freely moving animals.'

result: In Paradigm 1, the majority of mice (7/12) displayed appropriate memory recall at 1 mA intensity and six shocks, though variability was observed. Increasing shock amplitude from 0.6 to 1 mA significantly enhanced fear discrimination and freezing behavior. Fear discrimination was most prominent on Recall Day 1 and returned to baseline by Recall Day 2.
evaluation: Reviewers acknowledged the variability in responses and the optimization of shock parameters without critique. One reviewer noted the study 'sets the initial parameters and neuronal validation needed to further optimize a head-fixed CFC paradigm that produces freezing,' implicitly accepting these parameter-testing results as valid contributions to paradigm development.

result: In Paradigm 2 using two novel VR environments, significant differences between Control and CFC VRs were observed only for first lap freezing, not for average freezing or lap completion time across all laps. After the first lap, mice showed similar freezing in both environments, indicating rapid fear extinction within the first recall session.
evaluation: Reviewers were critical of Paradigm 2's effectiveness. One stated 'Version 2 showed no clear evidence of learning - average freezing at recall day 1 was not different than pre-shock freezing. First lap freezing showed a difference, but this single lap effect is not useful for many of the neural circuit questions for which this paradigm is meant to facilitate.' This indicates the reviewers found the evidence insufficient for demonstrating robust contextual fear learning.

result: Paradigm 3, which kept the tail-coat on during recall and used shorter inter-shock intervals, showed better fear discrimination than Paradigm 2 with significant freezing in both first lap and average across all laps. Mice maintained discrimination for the first two recall days with delayed extinction compared to Paradigm 2, though the effect size for first lap freezing was weaker than Paradigms 1 and 2 while average freezing showed a strong effect.
evaluation: Reviewers acknowledged Paradigm 3's improvements over Paradigm 2, stating 'Version 3 produces greater freezing and slower extinction than version 2. While the magnitude of the context discrimination is less than that in version 1, further optimization of the VR CFC is likely to produce robust learning and extinction.' This indicates acceptance of the claims while noting room for optimization.

result: Following fear conditioning, hippocampal CA1 place cells showed remapping, with a subset remaining stable while others changed their preferred firing locations. Remapping occurred in both the Familiar and CFC VR to similar extents, paralleling findings in freely moving animals.
evaluation: Reviewers explicitly validated these findings, stating 'The results support this aim and largely replicate previous findings in freely moving subjects.' One reviewer noted 'One difference from previous work of note is that VR CFC led to remapping of the control environment, not just the conditioning context,' acknowledging this as a difference but not challenging the validity of the remapping observations themselves.

result: There was an increase in the number of place cells in the CFC VR during memory recall, and place cells had narrower fields in the CFC VR during memory recall. No significant differences were found in lap-by-lap reliability and out-of-field firing of place cells.
evaluation: Reviewers accepted these place cell findings as part of the validation of the paradigm. One stated the study demonstrates 'hippocampal neuron remapping during fear learning and extinction, the study highlights the paradigm's utility for exploring memory dynamics.' The increased place cell numbers and narrower fields were not challenged, indicating reviewer acceptance of these novel observations.

result: The cylindrical treadmill setup enabled detection of additional conditioned responses beyond freezing, including hesitation and backward movement. Mild electric shock applied to the tail triggered freezing behavior as the conditioned response in head-fixed mice, making the paradigm more comparable to freely moving paradigms than previous air-puff methods.
evaluation: Reviewers explicitly acknowledged this methodological advance, with one stating the authors 'developed a contextual fear learning (CFC) paradigm in head-fixed mice that produces freezing as the conditioned response' and noting this addresses limitations of prior methods where 'lick suppression is the conditioned response' which 'does not easily allow comparison of head-fixed studies with extensive previous work in freely moving animals.'

result: The choice of neutral environment influenced fear discrimination, with mice freezing more in the fear-conditioned VR when the neutral environment was familiar (Paradigm 1) rather than novel (Paradigms 2 and 3).
evaluation: Reviewers explicitly discussed this finding, noting 'Paradigm versions 1 and 2 vary the familiarity of the control context' and that 'Version 1 is the most promising' while 'Version 2 showed no clear evidence of learning.' This comparative assessment indicates reviewer acceptance of the claim that environmental familiarity affects fear discrimination.

result: The authors acknowledge several limitations: the head-fixed CFC paradigm is less naturalistic than freely moving CFC, contexts were defined only by visual cues while other sensory cues remained constant, mice were water-restricted throughout, the advancement criterion excluded less adept runners requiring larger cohorts, and few female mice reached the experimental stage due to weight loss concerns.
evaluation: Reviewers acknowledged these limitations, with one noting 'the authors note the limitations of this study' in the discussion. Another reviewer specifically highlighted 'Extended training and attrition rate: the paradigm requires weeks of training and only 40% of mice reach criteria' as a weakness. The reviewers' recognition of these limitations without disputing them indicates acceptance of the authors' self-assessment.

result: Background claims establishing the rationale for the study, including capabilities of multi-photon imaging, limitations of head-fixation, standard CFC procedures, hippocampal role in memory, place cell properties, and prior findings on place cell remapping and narrowing after fear conditioning.
evaluation: These background claims were not challenged by reviewers and serve as the established scientific context for the study. Reviewers accepted the rationale that the approach 'provides a way to perform multiphoton imaging of neural circuits, and other techniques that are typically performed in head-fixed animals, during behaviors that have traditionally been studied in freely moving animals.'
